name: Panthenol

lead: Panthenol is a vitamin B5 derivative found in moisturisers, shampoos, lip care and healing ointments. It is used to hydrate skin, calm irritation and leave skin and hair feeling softer and smoother.

Skin converts it to pantothenic acid, which is used to make coenzyme A, and it binds water as a humectant. Studies and reviews describe hydration and post-procedure wound-healing roles for dexpanthenol; hair-growth claims lack trial support in the sources reviewed.

paras: It is applied in leave-on moisturisers and serums, as an ingredient in conditioners and shampoos, and in ointments such as Bepanthen for dry, irritated or healing skin. It is a routine ingredient in barrier and post-procedure care.
It is generally well tolerated; rare contact dermatitis or allergy has been reported.

angle.text: Panthenol converts to vitamin B5 in the skin and draws water in as a humectant, so it goes into moisturisers, hair products and wound creams. Skin looks softer and calmer, and human data mainly cover hydration and wound healing.

lead: Panthenol is the alcohol analogue of pantothenic acid (vitamin B5). Skin and mucous membranes convert it to pantothenic acid, so it is classed as a provitamin; dexpanthenol is the biologically active D form, while cosmetic ingredient lists may use D-panthenol or a racemic DL mixture.[1][2]

People use it to look better through the skin barrier and the hair fibre. In moisturisers, lip balms and masks it acts as a humectant that helps skin hold water, so skin looks smoother and less flaky; in shampoos and conditioners it is added for hair thickness, body and shine; and in wound-care ointments such as Bepanthen it is used to support healing after minor injuries and cosmetic procedures such as laser resurfacing, which affects how quickly skin returns to an even appearance.[1][3][4][5]

Published research includes laboratory work on gene expression in skin cells, controlled studies of moisturising formulations, reviews of post-procedure wound healing, and randomised trials of finished products that contain panthenol alongside other ingredients.[3][4][6][5][7] It is generally well tolerated; contact allergy is uncommon but reported, with patch-test positivity rates described as rising in recent years.[1][8]

paras: Panthenol (C9H19NO4, molar mass about 205 g/mol) is a viscous, colourless, odourless liquid that dissolves easily in water and alcohol. It exists as two enantiomers; only D-panthenol (dexpanthenol) is biologically active, which is why cosmetic and pharmaceutical products specify the D form or a DL mixture.[1]

Panthenol penetrates skin and mucous membranes and is rapidly oxidised to pantothenic acid, a building block of coenzyme A, which takes part in fatty-acid synthesis and many enzymatic reactions and in cell growth.[1][2] Reviews of wound-healing research report that topical dexpanthenol upregulates genes involved in the healing process in laboratory and clinical studies, and that cultured human fibroblasts show altered gene expression with calcium pantothenate.[4][9]

Cosmetic chemistry describes panthenol as a humectant that attracts water and reduces transepidermal water loss, which is the rationale for its inclusion in moisturisers and barrier-repair products.[1][2][10]

Panthenol appears in moisturisers, lip balms, facial masks, shampoos, conditioners and styling products.[1][2][10] Skin-care brands combine it with ceramides, allantoin and similar barrier ingredients for post-procedure and sensitive-skin lines.[6][5]

For hair, manufacturers describe it as adding thickness, body and smoothness to the strand. A 2026 paper used spectroscopic techniques to study how panthenol interacts with hair fibres and reported mechanistic evidence of strengthening.[11] Forum posts on T Nation, for example, mention panthenol alongside biotin in shampoos marketed to athletes for hair thickness.[12]

Dexpanthenol ointments such as Bepanthen are used on minor wounds, nappy rash, dry and irritated skin and after procedures.[1][4] Registered trials have also studied it in diabetic foot ulcers and in mouthwash for radiation-related oral mucositis.[13][14]

A 2011 controlled clinical study in the Journal of Cosmetic Science examined the skin-moisturising effects of panthenol-based formulations.[3] A 2020 review of PubMed and Embase literature concluded that in vitro and clinical studies show topical dexpanthenol promotes superficial and post-procedure wound healing, including rapid re-epithelialisation and restoration of barrier function.[4] A clinical-dermatology overview of common cosmeceuticals also discusses it among widely used skin ingredients.[10]

For hair, finished products containing panthenol have been tested as part of combinations. A 24-week randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of a scalp antioxidant and barrier-enhancing cosmetic regimen examined scalp condition and shedding,[15] and a randomised trial of a combination of heat-treated Limosilactobacillus fermentum LM1020 with menthol, salicylic acid and panthenol examined hair growth and the scalp microbiome in androgenetic alopecia.[7] Because these are multi-ingredient products, the results describe the combination rather than panthenol alone.

Wikipedia describes panthenol as generally well tolerated, with rare reports of skin irritation, contact dermatitis and contact allergy, and low acute toxicity in animal studies.[1] A 2025 review in Dermatitis reports that panthenol allergy is uncommon but that patch-test positivity has risen from roughly 0.2 to 0.7 percent to about 1.2 percent in recent years, and it notes cases in which products tested as-is were positive before the individual ingredient was identified. The authors call for more frequent testing of the allergen.[8]

Panthenol is a common ingredient in mass-market and pharmacy skin and hair products worldwide and is a staple of hypoallergenic and dermocosmetic marketing.[8] Bepanthen is a well-known brand of dexpanthenol ointment in Europe.[1] In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding forums it comes up mostly as an ingredient to look for in hair-care products, rather than as a topic of its own.[12]

A 2011 controlled clinical study examined skin moisturising effects of panthenol-based formulations.[3] A 2020 review summarised in vitro and clinical studies of dexpanthenol after medical and cosmetic procedures.[4] A 2025 double-blind randomised controlled study evaluated a panthenol-enriched mask for skin barrier recovery after facial laser treatment,[5] and a 2024 randomised trial in people with actinic keratosis tested a prebiotic and panthenol-containing dermocosmetic for tolerance of daylight photodynamic therapy.[16] Registered trials include Bepanthen ointment versus petrolatum after laser therapy (NCT03095872),[6] an 80-person phase 3 trial of an ointment in diabetic foot ulcers (NCT02379468),[13] and a phase 2 study of dexpanthenol mouthwash for radiation oral mucositis (NCT01318889).[14] Hair trials involve multi-ingredient products.[7][15]
